edges.title: Nielsen’s inscription of his First Symphony to Brahms

works.from: Symphony No. 1 in G minor, Op. 7 (score inscribed “in tiefster Verehrung”)
works.to: Brahms’s remark on the symphony, relayed by William Behrend, December 1895

edges.claim: On 7 November 1894 Dr Eduard Schiff took Nielsen to [[brahms]] in Vienna, and Brahms asked to keep the symphony and the F minor String Quartet to look through. Nielsen wrote to him on 25 December. A copy of the First Symphony in the archive of the Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde in Vienna is inscribed to Brahms “in tiefster Verehrung”, in deepest veneration. Brahms did not reply in writing. In December 1895 the critic William Behrend, visiting him, heard him recall a new Danish symphony in G minor, by “a Hansen”, and say that it was good; Behrend brought Nielsen thanks and appreciative remarks.

edges.title: Nielsen and the Ring at Dresden

works.from: Der Ring des Nibelungen, Dresden, September 1890

edges.claim: On his first stay in Germany, on an Ancker grant, Nielsen heard the four operas of the Ring at Dresden in September 1890. His diary for 10 September, after Das Rheingold, reads: “The musician who does not think [[wagner]] great is himself very small.” After Siegfried on 13 September he wrote that the first act was the most manly and energetic music ever written and that it “sparks with steel and swords”. Knud Ketting notes that Nielsen later modified this view considerably.

edges.title: Mozart rehearsal and the Wind Quintet

works.from: A Mozart piece for piano and winds, rehearsed at Christian Christiansen’s home, autumn 1921

edges.claim: In the autumn of 1921 Nielsen telephoned the pianist Christian Christiansen while he was rehearsing a Mozart piece with four members of the Copenhagen Wind Quintet. The players went on playing, Nielsen asked to come and listen, and soon afterwards he told the oboist Svend Christian Felumb that he would like to write a quintet for them. Knud Ketting writes that Nielsen heard how [[mozart]], above all in the variations of the last movement, plays with the character of each instrument. The Wind Quintet, finished in April 1922, ends with a set of variations.
edges.note: The Carl Nielsen Edition, following Torben Meyer, says only that Nielsen was inspired by hearing the Copenhagen Wind Quintet play a piece by Mozart at Christiansen’s home, and thinks it was probably the Quintet for piano and winds, K. 452. Ketting names Mozart’s Sinfonia Concertante and gives the telephone call. He cites no source for it.

edges.title: Liszt’s sonata and the Fourth Symphony’s single span
edges.claim: Knud Ketting writes that the idea of one large work without separate movements is said to have come from [[liszt]]’s B minor Sonata, which Nielsen’s friend Henrik Knudsen had played to him. Nielsen began the Fourth Symphony in 1914 and conducted the first performance on 1 February 1916. Its four sections, Allegro, Poco allegretto, Poco adagio quasi andante and Allegro, are played without a break.
edges.note: Ketting gives the story as hearsay (“is said to have come from”) and names no letter or diary. No document by Nielsen that mentions Liszt’s sonata has been consulted.
